In [[mathematics]], the '''Fourier transform on finite groups''' is a generalization of the [[discrete Fourier transform]] from [[cyclic group|cyclic]] to arbitrary [[finite group]]s.

==Definitions==
The '''Fourier transform''' of a function <math>f : G \to \Complex</math> at a [[representation of a finite group|representation]] <math>\varrho : G \to \mathrm{GL}_{d_\varrho}(\Complex)</math> of <math>G</math> is

<math display="block">
\widehat{f}(\varrho) = \sum_{a \in G} f(a) \varrho(a).
</math>

For each representation <math>\varrho</math> of <math>G</math>, <math>\widehat{f}(\varrho)</math> is a <math>d_\varrho \times d_\varrho</math> matrix, where <math>d_\varrho</math> is the degree of <math>\varrho</math>.

Let <math>\widehat{G}</math> be the complete set of inequivalent [[Irreducible representation|irreducible representations]] of <math>G</math>. Then the '''inverse Fourier transform''' at an element <math>a</math> of <math>G</math> is given by

<math display="block">
f(a) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{\varrho \in \widehat{G}} d_{\varrho} \mathrm{Tr}\left(\varrho(a^{-1})\widehat{f}(\varrho)\right).
</math>

==Properties==

===Transform of a convolution===
The '''convolution''' of two functions <math>f, g : G \to \mathbb{C}</math> is defined as

<math display="block">
(f \ast g)(a) = \sum_{b \in G} f\!\left(ab^{-1}\right) g(b).
</math>

The Fourier transform of a convolution at any representation <math>\varrho</math> of <math>G</math> is given by

<math display="block">
\widehat{f \ast g}(\varrho) = \hat{f}(\varrho)\hat{g}(\varrho).
</math>

===Plancherel formula===
For functions <math>f, g : G \to \mathbb{C}</math>, the Plancherel formula states

<math display="block">
\sum_{a \in G} f(a^{-1}) g(a) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_i d_{\varrho_i} \text{Tr}\left(\hat{f}(\varrho_i)\hat{g}(\varrho_i)\right),
</math>

where <math>\varrho_i</math> are the irreducible representations of <math>G</math>.

==Fourier transform for finite abelian groups==
If the group ''G'' is a finite [[abelian group]], the situation simplifies considerably:

* all irreducible representations <math>\varrho_i</math> are of degree 1 and hence equal to the irreducible characters of the group. Thus the matrix-valued Fourier transform becomes scalar-valued in this case.

* The set of irreducible ''G''-representations has a natural group structure in its own right, which can be identified with the group <math>\widehat G := \mathrm{Hom}(G, S^1)</math> of [[group homomorphisms]] from ''G'' to <math>S^1 = \{z \in \mathbb C, |z|=1\}</math>. This group is known as the [[Pontryagin dual]] of ''G''.

The Fourier transform of a function <math>f : G \to \mathbb{C}</math> is the function <math>\widehat{f}: \widehat{G}\to \mathbb{C}</math> given by

<math display="block">
\widehat{f}(\chi) = \sum_{a \in G} f(a) \bar{\chi}(a).
</math>

The inverse Fourier transform is then given by

<math display="block">
f(a) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{\chi \in \widehat{G}} \widehat{f}(\chi) \chi(a).
</math>
For <math>G = \mathbb Z/n \mathbb Z</math>, a choice of a primitive ''n''-th [[root of unity]] <math>\zeta</math> yields an isomorphism

<math display="block">G \to \widehat G,</math>

given by <math>m \mapsto (r \mapsto \zeta^{mr})</math>. In the literature, the common choice is <math>\zeta = e^{2 \pi i /n}</math>, which explains the formula given in the article about the [[discrete Fourier transform]]. However, such an isomorphism is not canonical, similarly to the situation that a finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to its [[dual vector space|dual]], but giving an isomorphism requires choosing a basis.

A property that is often useful in probability is that the Fourier transform of the uniform distribution is simply <math>\delta_{a,0}</math>, where 0 is the group identity and <math>\delta_{i,j}</math> is the [[Kronecker delta]].

Fourier Transform can also be done on cosets of a group.

==Relationship with representation theory==
There is a direct relationship between the Fourier transform on finite groups and the [[representation theory of finite groups]]. The set of complex-valued functions on a finite group, <math>G</math>, together with the operations of pointwise addition and convolution, form a ring that is naturally identified with the [[group ring]] of <math>G</math> over the complex numbers, <math>\mathbb{C}[G]</math>. [[Module_(mathematics)|Modules]] of this ring are the same thing as representations. [[Maschke's theorem]] implies that <math>\mathbb{C}[G]</math> is a [[semisimple ring]], so by the [[Artin–Wedderburn theorem]] it decomposes as a [[product of rings|direct product]] of [[matrix ring]]s. The Fourier transform on finite groups explicitly exhibits this decomposition, with a matrix ring of dimension <math>d_\varrho</math> for each irreducible representation.
More specifically, the [[Peter-Weyl theorem]] (for finite groups) states that there is an isomorphism
<math display="block">\mathbb C[G] \cong \bigoplus_{i} \mathrm{End}(V_i)</math>
given by
<math display="block">\sum_{g \in G} a_g g \mapsto \left(\sum a_g \rho_i(g): V_i \to V_i\right)</math>
The left hand side is the [[group ring|group algebra]] of ''G''. The direct sum is over a complete set of inequivalent irreducible ''G''-representations <math>\varrho_i : G \to \mathrm{GL}(V_i)</math>.

The Fourier transform for a finite group is just this isomorphism. The product formula mentioned above is equivalent to saying that this map is a [[ring isomorphism]].

== Over other fields ==

The above representation theoretic decomposition can be generalized to fields <math>k</math> other than <math>\mathbb{C}</math> as long as <math>\text{char}(k) \nmid |G|</math> via [[Maschke's theorem]]. That is, the group algebra <math>k[G]</math> is semisimple. The same formulas may be used for the Fourier transform and its inverse, as crucially <math>\frac{1}{|G|}</math> is defined in <math>k</math>.

== Modular case ==

When <math>\text{char}(k) \mid |G|</math>, <math>k[G]</math> is no longer semisimple and one must consider the modular representation theory of <math>G</math> over <math>k</math>. We can still decompose the group algebra into blocks via the [[Peirce decomposition]] using idempotents. That is

<math>k[G] \cong \bigoplus_i k[G]e_i</math>

and <math>1 = \sum_i e_i</math> is a decomposition of the identity into central, primitive, orthogonal idempotents. Choosing a basis for the blocks <math>\text{span}_k \{g e_i | g \in G\}</math> and writing the projection maps <math>v \mapsto v e_i</math> as a matrix yields the modular [[DFT matrix]].<ref>{{cite arxiv|last=Walters|first=Jackson|title=The Modular DFT of the Symmetric Group  |date=2024|eprint=2404.05796|class=math.RT}}</ref>

For example, for the symmetric group the idempotents of <math>F_p[S_n]</math> are computed in Murphy<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Murphy |first1=G.E. |date= 1983|title=The idempotents of the symmetric group and Nakayama's conjecture |journal=Journal of Algebra |volume=81 |issue=1 |pages=258–265 |doi=10.1016/0021-8693(83)90219-3 }}</ref> and explicitly in SageMath.<ref>SageMath, the Sage Mathematics Software System (Version 10.4.0), The Sage Developers, 2024, https://www.sagemath.org.</ref>

==Unitarity==

One can normalize the above definition to obtain

<math>\hat{f}(\rho)=\sqrt{\frac{d_\rho}{|G|}}\sum_{g \in G}f(g)\rho(g)</math>

with inverse 

<math>f(g)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|G|}}\sum_{\rho \in \widehat{G}}\sqrt{d_\rho}\mathrm{Tr}(\hat{f}(\rho)\rho^{-1}(g))</math>.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1145/258533.258548 |chapter=Quantum computation of Fourier transforms over symmetric groups |title=Proceedings of the twenty-ninth annual ACM symposium on Theory of computing - STOC '97 |date=1997 |last1=Beals |first1=Robert |pages=48–53 |isbn=0-89791-888-6 }}</ref> 

Two representations are considered equivalent if one may be obtained from the other by a change of basis. This is an equivalence relation, and each equivalence class contains a unitary representation. The unitary representations can be obtained via Weyl's [[unitarian trick]] in characteristic zero. If <math>\widehat{G}</math> consists of unitary representations, then the corresponding DFT will be unitary. 

Over finite fields <math>F_{q^2}</math>, it is possible to find a change of basis in certain cases, for example the symmetric group, by decomposing the matrix <math>U</math> associated to a <math>G</math>-invariant [[symmetric bilinear form]] as <math>U=AA^*</math>, where <math>^*</math> denotes conjugate-transpose with respect to <math>x \mapsto x^q</math> conjugation. The unitary representation is given by <math>A^*\rho(g)A^{* -1}</math>. To obtain the unitary DFT, note that as defined above <math>DFT.DFT^* = S</math>, where <math>S</math> is a [[diagonal matrix]] consisting of +1's and -1's. We can factor <math>S=RR^*</math> by factoring each sign <math>c_i = z_i z_i^*</math>. <math>uDFT = R^{-1}.DFT</math> is unitary.

==Applications==

This generalization of the discrete Fourier transform is used in [[numerical analysis]]. A [[circulant matrix]] is a matrix where every column is a [[cyclic shift]] of the previous one. Circulant matrices can be [[Matrix diagonalization|diagonalized]] quickly using the [[fast Fourier transform]], and this  yields a fast method for solving [[system of linear equations|systems of linear equations]] with circulant matrices. Similarly, the Fourier transform on arbitrary groups can be used to give fast algorithms for matrices with other symmetries {{harv|Åhlander|Munthe-Kaas|2005}}. These algorithms can be used for the construction of [[numerical partial differential equations|numerical methods for solving partial differential equations]] that preserve the symmetries of the equations {{harv|Munthe-Kaas|2006}}.

When applied to the [[Boolean group]] <math>(\mathbb Z / 2 \mathbb Z)^n</math>, the Fourier transform on this group is the [[Hadamard transform]], which is  commonly used in [[quantum computing]] and other fields. [[Shor's algorithm]] uses both the Hadamard transform (by applying a [[Hadamard gate]] to every qubit) as well as the [[quantum Fourier transform]]. The former considers the qubits as indexed by the group <math>(\mathbb Z / 2 \mathbb Z)^n</math> and the later considers them as indexed by <math>\mathbb Z / 2^n \mathbb Z</math> for the purpose of the Fourier transform on finite groups.<ref>[https://www.cse.iitk.ac.in/users/rmittal/prev_course/s19/reports/5_algo.pdf Lecture 5: Basic quantum algorithms, Rajat Mittal, pp. 4-9]</ref>
